lines.cap: **Narrator:** Thursday, dusk. The Banyan Hill library has updated its sign. Will is ignoring it, because another ghost has moved in.
**The Ghost:** I am thy father's spirit, doom'd for a certain term to walk the night—
**Will:** Excuse me! ONE ghost per air-conditioned library! Besides, I **played** you at the Globe in **1600**!
**Hamlet:** To kopi, or not to kopi: that is the question. Whether 'tis nobler to drink iced Milo...
**Mei:** Bro, the canteen Auntie has been waiting twenty minutes. Pick a drink! **One star** for speed.
**Polonius:** Aha! Behind this curtain, I deduce the prince is mad with love — or caffeine!
**Mr H:** Step away from the curtains, Polonius. That ends badly for you in **Act 3**.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode three: To Be or Not to Be (Late).
**Mr H:** **Hamlet**, written around **1600**, is a **revenge tragedy** set at **Elsinore**, the royal castle of Denmark.
**Nib:** The Elizabethan revenge recipe: a **ghost**, a hero who **delays**, **feigned madness**, a **play-within-a-play**, and a bloodbath at the end.
**Hamlet:** My father died suddenly. Within **two months**, my mother **Gertrude** married his brother **Claudius** — my uncle AND new stepfather!
**Hamlet:** Denmark feels like '**an unweeded garden / That grows to seed**'. 'Frailty, thy name is woman!'
**Mr H:** Midnight on the battlements. As Hamlet follows the Ghost, the guard **Marcellus** — **not** Hamlet! — speaks a famous line:
**Will:** 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.'
**Nib:** Zoom in! '**Rotten**' starts an image pattern of **decay, disease and poison**. And '**state**' puns on both the nation and its condition.
**The Ghost:** Claudius poured **poison** in my sleeping ear! 'The serpent that did sting thy father's life / Now wears his crown.'
**Mei:** Okay, if a glowing armoured dad tells you who murdered him, why not arrest Claudius on Monday morning?
**Mr H:** **Context**. The Ghost describes **purgatory**, a Catholic belief. Protestant audiences feared a ghost '**May be the devil**' luring Hamlet to hell.
**Nib:** Plus the **divine right of kings**: killing an anointed monarch is **regicide**, a sin against God. Hamlet needs **proof**.
**Mr H:** At Elsinore, nobody is what they appear. That's the theme of **appearance versus reality**.
**Hamlet:** Everyone wears wedding silks; I stay in mourning black. 'Seems, madam! nay it is; I know not "seems."'
**Hamlet:** Claudius beams like a kindly uncle, yet 'one may smile, and smile, and be a villain'. So I put an '**antic disposition**' on.
**Mei:** '**Antic disposition**' — pretending to act mad so nobody suspects what you know! Wait... is he ONLY pretending?
**Polonius:** Before my son **Laertes** sails for Paris, I give wise counsel: 'This above all: to thine own self be true.'
**Nib:** Deeply **ironic**, darling: the man preaching honesty spies on his own children and everyone else!
**Polonius:** Even I notice Hamlet's 'mad' insults are suspiciously sharp: 'Though this be madness, yet there is method in't.'
**Mr H:** Claudius recruits Hamlet's school friends **Rosencrantz and Guildenstern** as spies. Only **Horatio** stays truly loyal.
**Will:** Then travelling actors arrive! Hamlet stages **The Mousetrap**, a play copying the ear-poisoning — **metatheatre**, fiction exposing truth!
**Hamlet:** 'The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.' Claudius panics and storms out. Proof!
**Mei:** Using a school play as a lie detector? Okay, **two stars**.

chapters.title: To be, or not to be — and why wait?

lines.cap: **Mr H:** **Act 3 Scene 1**. First, put that skull down, Hamlet — there is **NO skull** in 'To be, or not to be'! That's **Act 5**.
**Hamlet:** Sorry. Poster habit. Ahem: 'To be, or not to be: that is the question:'
**Nib:** **Antithesis**: setting opposites side by side — **to be** versus **not to be**; **suffer** versus **take arms**.
**Hamlet:** 'Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer / The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, / Or to take arms against a sea of troubles'
**Kevin:** Look at all those colons and mid-line pauses! Every **caesura** slows him down as his thoughts turn back on themselves!
**Mr H:** What stops us ending our suffering? Fear of '**The undiscover'd country**' after death. Notice Hamlet never says 'I' — only '**we**' and '**us**'.
**Hamlet:** 'Thus conscience does make cowards of us all'... resolution is 'sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought'.
**Mei:** Then in **Act 3 Scene 3**, you catch Claudius kneeling alone! Why don't you strike?!
**Hamlet:** If I kill him while he's praying, his soul goes straight to **heaven**! How is that revenge?
**Nib:** Peak **dramatic irony**! Once Hamlet leaves, Claudius admits he couldn't repent: 'My words fly up, my thoughts remain below'.
**Mr H:** Compare Hamlet's two **foils**, fellow grieving sons: **Laertes** rages instantly and gets manipulated; **Fortinbras** marches steadily.
**Polonius:** And when Hamlet DOES act on impulse in Gertrude's closet, he stabs ME behind the tapestry! Not ideal!

chapters.title: Rosemary, Yorick and the poisoned cup

lines.cap: **Ophelia:** Let's talk about **women and power**. My father Polonius and brother Laertes order me to reject Hamlet. I say: 'I shall obey, my lord.'
**Nib:** They use her as bait to spy on Hamlet. Then Hamlet kills her father, and in **Act 4** Ophelia's **real madness** shatters into **prose** and song.
**Ophelia:** 'There's rosemary, that's for remembrance.' My helplessness is a tragic **foil** to Hamlet's chosen act — before I drown.
**Narrator:** **Act 5 Scene 1**. A graveyard. NOW Hamlet may hold the skull.
**Hamlet:** 'Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio' — NOT 'I knew him well'! Yorick was the court jester who carried me as a child.
**Mr H:** **Mortality**: death is the **great leveller**. Jester and emperor — even Alexander the Great — return to the same **dust**.
**Hamlet:** Returning from sea, I'm calmer. '**The readiness is all.**' Claudius rigs a fencing match with **Laertes**: a **poisoned sword** and a **poisoned cup**.
**Will:** Gertrude defies Claudius and drinks the cup! The poisoned rapier wounds **both** Laertes and Hamlet! Hamlet finally kills Claudius!
**Hamlet:** Horatio lives to tell my story; **Fortinbras** of Norway takes the crown. My last words end four hours of talk: '**The rest is silence.**'
**Mei:** Three stars! Tragic, poetic, and Claudius got poisoned twice.
**Narrator:** Friday. Mr Hargreaves has reached Mug Ten. It says 'TO TEA OR NOT TO TEA', and today it is topical.
**Nib:** First, Hamlet's five great soliloquies in order: **S**ome **R**eal **T**hinkers **N**ever **A**ct — **Solid flesh, Rogue, To be, Now might I, All occasions**.
**Mei:** And the seven themes: **W A R M, C A M**. **Women, Action vs thought, Revenge, Madness, Corruption, Appearance vs reality, Mortality**!
**Mr H:** Exam question: **How does Shakespeare present Hamlet's mind in 'To be, or not to be'?** Mei — climb the ladder.
**Mei:** **Point**: Shakespeare presents Hamlet as a mind **paralysed by over-thinking**, not simply a coward.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: he weighs whether to suffer '**The slings and arrows**' or fight '**a sea of troubles**', concluding '**conscience does make cowards of us all**'.
**Mei:** **Explain**: the military metaphor feels relentless, '**sea**' makes life's problems impossibly vast, and using '**us**' instead of 'I' turns delay into a universal law.
**Mei:** **Link**: the speech itself dramatises **thought versus action**, showing resolution '**sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought**'.
**Mr H:** Not one plot retelling. Embedded quotes, pronoun analysis, linked to theme. Will, stop crying on the books.
**Will:** I'm not crying. The library aircon is in my eye.
**Narrator:** Before Fortinbras marches into Room 8H, here are your memory hooks and six Hamlet exam traps.
**Mei:** Soliloquies: **Some Real Thinkers Never Act**. Themes: **W A R M, C A M**. Deaths in order: **Please Only Get Charlie's Lunch, Hamlet!**
**The Ghost:** One! '**Something is rotten in the state of Denmark**' is spoken by the guard **Marcellus** in **Act 1 Scene 4**, NOT Hamlet!
**Hamlet:** Two! **No skull** in 'To be, or not to be'! That's **Act 3 Scene 1**; Yorick's skull is **Act 5 Scene 1**.
**Will:** Three! Quote accurately: '**Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio**' — never 'I knew him well'!
**Polonius:** Four! Don't call Hamlet's madness simply fake OR simply real. Argue that his **antic disposition** blurs into real grief!
**Nib:** Five! Not every speech is a **soliloquy**! 'What a piece of work is a man' is spoken to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.
**Ophelia:** Six! The play **never** proves Gertrude knew about the murder. Leave her guilt open, just as the text does.
**Mei:** Final rating for Hamlet: **four stars**. Masterpiece, iconic speeches, minus one star because you stabbed the curtain guy by mistake.
**Polonius:** Honestly, very fair.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Who actually says '**Something is rotten in the state of Denmark**'?
**The Ghost:** **Marcellus**, a guard on the battlements in **Act 1 Scene 4** — not Hamlet!
**Mr H:** Why does Hamlet stage **The Mousetrap** play in **Act 3**?
**Hamlet:** To test **Claudius's guilt** — in case the Ghost '**May be the devil**'.
**Mr H:** Why does Hamlet spare Claudius in the **prayer scene** (**Act 3 Scene 3**), and why is it **dramatic irony**?
**Nib:** Hamlet fears sending Claudius's soul to **heaven** — yet **we** hear Claudius admit his prayer fails!
**Mr H:** Which two grieving sons act as **foils** to Hamlet's delay?
**Ophelia:** **Laertes** and **Fortinbras**.
**Mr H:** Complete Hamlet's famous graveyard line in **Act 5 Scene 1**: '**Alas, poor Yorick!** I knew him...'
**Will:** '...**Horatio**!' Never 'well'.
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Hamlet** quiz in your English Lab.
**The Ghost:** This library air-conditioning is glorious. I shall haunt Shelf B.
**Will:** Shelf B is SONNETS! Get your own school, Dad-Ghost!
